outcome: Two events since 26 January 2024 bear on the problem: Alekseyev's arXiv:2601.17832 (25 Jan 2026) lifts the computational lower bound on a quasiperfect number from 10³⁵ to 10⁴⁵, and Toyohara, Tao and Yao's arXiv:2608.02066 (3 Aug 2026) claims that any quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors, using an AI-assisted computation whose main step cannot yet be replayed; no quasiperfect number is known and existence remains open.
problem_asks: One question: does there exist a natural number n with σ(n) = 2n+1, where σ(n) is the sum of all divisors of n (a quasiperfect number)? Part (i): existence of at least one such n. The statement asks for nothing else: no size bound, no count, no structure, no classification. A single example, or a proof that none exists, would settle it. Properties that a hypothetical example must have are not requested by the statement; they are context for it.

events.what_happened: P. Cattaneo, 'Sui numeri quasiperfetti', Boll. Un. Mat. Ital. (3) 6 (1951), 59–62. Cited in arXiv:2608.02066 as [1] and in secondary sources as the origin of the result that a quasiperfect number must be an odd square. I did not open the 1951 paper itself.
events.delivers: Any quasiperfect number is an odd perfect square (the square and oddness restriction).
events.direction: Restriction on the shape of any hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: H. L. Abbott, C. E. Aull, E. Brown and D. Suryanarayana, 'Quasiperfect numbers', Acta Arith. 22 (1973), 439–447 (corrigendum Acta Arith. 29 (1976), 427–428). Known to me only from secondary sources: a 1980s paper by Graeme Cohen (quoted in a search summary) says the 1973 authors showed n > 10²⁰ and at least five distinct prime divisors; arXiv:2608.02066 cites its Theorem 3 as giving ω ≥ 8 when 3 does not divide n; Prasad and Sunitha (2017) cite it as giving ω ≥ 10 when gcd(N,15)=1. These three attributions do not agree. The 1973 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources only: n > 10²⁰ and ω(n) ≥ 5 in general; ω(n) ≥ 8 when 3 ∤ n (2608 attribution); ω(n) ≥ 10 when gcd(n,15)=1 (2017 attribution). Which of these the 1973 paper actually proves is unverified.
events.doubts: The three secondary descriptions of this paper's ω bounds conflict with each other (see disputes). Unopened original.
events.direction: Restrictions on the number of prime factors and on size of any hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: M. Kishore, 'Odd integers N with five distinct prime factors for which 2 − 10⁻¹² < σ(N)/N < 2 + 10⁻¹²', Math. Comp. 32 (1978), 303–309. Known from a search snippet of the AMS record and from a 1980 paper by Graeme Cohen quoted in a search summary: the 1978 paper establishes that a quasiperfect number has at least six distinct prime divisors (the summary also says it states there is no quasiperfect number with exactly five distinct prime factors). Kishore also announced the result in a 1975 Notices AMS abstract. The 1978 paper was not opened.
events.delivers: Per secondary sources: ω(n) ≥ 6 for any quasiperfect n (the step from five to six).
events.direction: Restriction on the number of prime factors of any hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: M. Kishore, 'On odd perfect, quasiperfect, and odd almost perfect numbers', Math. Comp. 36 (1981), 583–586. Known only from the AMS abstract as shown in a search snippet, which says it gives upper bounds for the six smallest prime factors of odd perfect, quasiperfect and odd almost perfect numbers. Not opened.
events.delivers: Per the abstract snippet only: upper bounds on the smallest prime factors of any hypothetical quasiperfect number. The exact bounds are unread.
events.direction: Restriction on prime factors of a hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: P. Hagis Jr. and G. L. Cohen, 'Some results concerning quasiperfect numbers', J. Austral. Math. Soc. Ser. A 33 (1982), 275–286 (DOI 10.1017/S1446788700018401; print issue October 1982). The abstract, as read through a summarising fetch of the Cambridge page, opens 'New methods are introduced here to show that if n is a quasiperfect number', then states n has at least seven distinct prime factors and n > 10³⁵; and that if 3 does not divide n, then at least nine distinct prime factors and n > 10⁴⁰. Search summaries describe the general computation as run on a CDC Cyber. The 2608 preprint says the ω ≥ 9 part was never published (see disputes). The 1982 paper itself was not readable.
events.delivers: For any quasiperfect n: ω(n) ≥ 7 and n > 10³⁵ (the general restriction stated on Wikipedia). The abstract also claims ω(n) ≥ 9 and n > 10⁴⁰ when 3 ∤ n; this claim is disputed by arXiv:2608.02066 and is not verified here.

checked_by.who: Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society (Series A)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; refereeing process not verified by me

events.directly_checkable: Not stated in the abstract. The argument is a hand proof combined with a long computer run (per secondary sources), so the computation is not directly checkable by hand.
events.doubts: The abstract's ω ≥ 9 claim for 3 ∤ n conflicts with arXiv:2608.02066's statement that this part was never published. Unresolved; the 1982 full text was not read.
events.direction: Restriction on any hypothetical example; the 3 ∤ n claim would be a stronger restriction if it holds. Does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: G. L. Cohen, 'The Nonexistence of Quasiperfect Numbers of Certain Forms', Fibonacci Quarterly vol. 20, issue 1 (1982); the scanned PDF at mathstat.dal.ca is a binary that my fetch could not read, so the content here comes from a search summary and is not verified. The summary says the paper shows that no perfect fourth power is quasiperfect, and no perfect sixth power prime to 3 is quasiperfect; for squares of squarefree m it could not rule out existence but showed such m would have more than 230,000 distinct prime factors (a search summary also gives t ≥ 230876 for a related exponent shape).
events.delivers: Per the summary only: nonexistence for quasiperfect fourth powers and for sixth powers prime to 3; for squares of squarefree numbers, a bound of more than 230,000 distinct prime factors. These are restrictions to subclasses and do not settle general existence.
events.remains: Existence in general, and the squares of squarefree numbers case.
events.doubts: Content unverified: the PDF could not be read by me.
events.direction: Partial nonexistence in special forms, plus a restriction on prime-factor count for one form; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: Forum thread 'Do Quasiperfect Numbers Really Exist?' on PhysicsForums (started 4–5 March 2012). The original poster, shown under the display name 'Joseph Fermat', claims to show that no quasiperfect number exists by rewriting σ(n) = 2n+1 in terms of a function h(n) and arguing that the resulting form is impossible; the attachment is not reproduced on the page. A reply from 'dodo' states that there is a problem going from eq. 8 to eq. 9, since 1 − (h(n) − 2) equals 3 − h(n), not the negative expression used. The original poster concedes that the proof is flawed and says they are back to the drawing board, without a corrected argument.
events.delivers: Claimed nonexistence of quasiperfect numbers. The argument fails at the step identified in the thread, and the poster concedes this.
events.remains: Everything: the claim was withdrawn in-thread without a repair.

checked_by.qualification: Reader who checked the algebra; qualifications not stated
checked_by.what_they_did: Identified an algebra error at the step from eq. 8 to eq. 9

events.directly_checkable: The algebra step is short and was checked in-thread; the attachment with the full argument is not reproduced.
events.doubts: The identified error at eq. 8 to eq. 9 was not repaired in the thread; the poster conceded.

withdrawn.what: The claimed nonexistence proof, conceded flawed by its poster in the thread

people: Forum poster shown as 'Joseph Fermat' (display name only)

events.what_happened: T. Yamada, 'On the divisibility of odd perfect numbers, quasiperfect numbers and amicable numbers by a high power of a prime', arXiv:1609.08795 (v1 28 Sep 2016; v2 8 Oct 2016; v3 9 Nov 2016; v4 12 Mar 2017; v5 29 Nov 2017; v6 7 Sep 2021). The abstract page gives journal reference INTEGERS 20 (2020), #A91. The abstract, read through a summarising fetch, gives explicit upper bounds for the smallest prime factor of multiperfect numbers of a specified form, and states 'We shall also give similar results for quasiperfect numbers'. The quasiperfect theorem itself was not read.
events.revisions: v1 28 Sep 2016; v2 8 Oct 2016; v3 9 Nov 2016; v4 12 Mar 2017; v5 29 Nov 2017; v6 7 Sep 2021 (last revised); journal INTEGERS 20 (2020) #A91.
events.delivers: Not established by my reading. Per the abstract only: an explicit upper bound on the smallest prime factor of quasiperfect numbers of a specified form with bounded exponents.
events.remains: Existence of any quasiperfect number, and the general case of the form.
events.direction: Restriction on the smallest prime factor of a specified form of hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: T. Yamada, 'Quasiperfect numbers with the same exponent', arXiv:1610.01063 (v1 4 Oct 2016; v2 8 Oct 2016; v3 29 Nov 2017, the current version; 11 pages). The abstract, read through a summarising fetch, says that if N = (p₁p₂⋯pₜ)^(2a) = m² is quasiperfect then 2a+1 is divisible by 3, and that N has at least one prime factor below exp(716.7944) (about 10³¹¹); it also gives lower bounds for quasiperfect numbers of the form m² with m squarefree. The abs page shows no journal reference. The theorems were not read.
events.revisions: v1 4 Oct 2016; v2 8 Oct 2016; v3 29 Nov 2017 (current).
events.delivers: Restricted to quasiperfect squares of the form (p₁⋯pₜ)^(2a): an exponent condition (3 divides 2a+1) and a prime factor below about 10³¹¹. Lower bounds for squares m² with m squarefree (values not read). Does not address non-square or other forms.
events.remains: Existence in general; the non-square case; the forms not covered by the lower bounds.
events.direction: Restrictions on a special form of any hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: V. Siva Rama Prasad and C. Sunitha, 'On quasiperfect numbers', Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics 23 (2017), no. 3, 73–78. Abstract as read through a summarising fetch: every quasiperfect number N has an odd number of 'special factors'; using this, ω(N) ≥ 15 when gcd(N,15)=1, which the abstract says refines Abbott et al.'s bound ω ≥ 10 for gcd(N,15)=1; and an alternate proof of Cohen's result for gcd(N,15)=5. The abstract's wording was quoted in part; the proofs were not read.
events.delivers: Under the extra hypothesis gcd(N,15)=1: ω(N) ≥ 15 (per the abstract). Restricted to the coprime-to-15 class; does not cover quasiperfect numbers divisible by 3 or 5.
events.remains: Existence in general; the case where 3 or 5 divides N.
events.doubts: arXiv:2608.02066's bibliography, as read, does not cite this paper, and it does not discuss a coprime-to-15 bound of 15. The 2017 proof was not checked by me. The GitHub repository fderuiter/quasiperfect repeats this bound as a conditional result.
events.direction: Restriction on the prime-factor count of a hypothetical example in the coprime-to-15 class; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: V. Siva Rama Prasad and C. Sunitha, 'On the prime factors of a quasiperfect number', Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics 25 (2019), no. 2, 16–21 (DOI 10.7546/nntdm.2019.25.2.16-21). Abstract as read through a summarising fetch: a lower bound on γ(N), the product of the distinct primes dividing N, in terms of r = ω(N); and every quasiperfect number is divisible by a prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4), with p ≡ 1 (mod 5) if 5 ∤ N and p ≡ 1 (mod 3) if 3 ∤ N.
events.delivers: Congruence restrictions on prime divisors of any quasiperfect number, and a lower bound on the product of its distinct primes in terms of ω. Restrictions only.
events.doubts: Not cited in arXiv:2608.02066's bibliography as read. The proofs were not checked.
events.direction: Restriction on prime divisors of a hypothetical example; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: B. Zemann, 'Quasi-Perfect Numbers Have at Least 8 Prime Divisors', viXra:2308.0024 (submitted 4 Aug 2023; the page lists 17 pages). The abstract says: 'By computation, it is shown that no quasi-perfect number has less than 8 prime divisors.' Per the 2026 preprint arXiv:2608.02066, the computation used a C++ implementation of the Hagis–Cohen interval-propagation method; the 2026 authors audited the public code and found an off-by-one error that silently skips 240 prime exponents, 35 of them feasible under the preprint's own criteria and never enumerated. The 2026 authors therefore say the 2023 work is not a complete proof. The viXra page shows no reviewer comments.
events.delivers: Claimed by computation: ω(n) ≥ 8 for any quasiperfect n. Per the 2026 audit, the enumeration skipped 35 feasible exponents, so the claim as a complete proof is contested. Restricted to ω; no existence claim.
events.remains: Existence of any quasiperfect number; the 35 unenumerated exponents, if the audit is right.

checked_by.who: Akira Toyohara, Ye Tao and Siqiong Yao (authors of arXiv:2608.02066)
checked_by.qualification: Authors of the competing 2026 preprint; they had access to Zemann's public code
checked_by.what_they_did: Audited the public code and reported an off-by-one coverage gap (35 feasible exponents never enumerated); judged the 2023 result not a complete proof while stating its conclusion is correct

events.directly_checkable: The claim is a computation; the code is public per the 2026 audit, which I did not inspect.
events.doubts: The coverage gap identified by the 2026 audit (35 feasible exponents never enumerated). Not peer reviewed (viXra). I did not find a response from Zemann.
events.direction: Claimed restriction ω(n) ≥ 8, the same claim as the 2026 Theorem 1, by a computation with a stated gap.

events.what_happened: OEIS A379490, 'Odd squares s such that 2*s is equal to bitwise-AND of 2*s and sigma(s)', created by Antti Karttunen on 13 Jan 2025. The entry notes that any quasiperfect number x (σ(x) = 2x+1) would occur in this sequence. On 19 Aug 2025 Giovanni Resta added a(4) and a(5) and stated a(6) > 4·10²¹. The five known terms are 399736269009, 1013616036225, 1393148751631700625, 2998748839068013955625 and 3547850289210724050225. Karttunen's comments ask about analogous sequences and note that such sequences would contain odd triperfect numbers if any exist.
events.revisions: Sequence created 13 Jan 2025; a(4), a(5) and the a(6) bound added 19 Aug 2025 (Resta).
events.delivers: A search bound on the candidate sequence: no further term below 4·10²¹. Any quasiperfect number would be a term, so this excludes quasiperfect numbers of this filtered form below 4·10²¹. The bound is subsumed by the 10⁴⁵ bound of arXiv:2601.17832.
events.remains: Existence of any quasiperfect number, including those above 4·10²¹ in this sequence.
events.directly_checkable: The terms are odd squares that can be checked by computing σ(s) directly.
events.direction: Restricts quasiperfect candidates of a bit-pattern form; does not answer existence.

events.what_happened: Max A. Alekseyev, 'Computing bounded solutions to linear Diophantine equations with the sum of divisors', arXiv:2601.17832, single author, v1 submitted 25 Jan 2026 (the only version listed on the abs page). The method finds all n ≤ U with aσ(n) = bn + c, implemented in SageMath with MapReduce parallelisation. The paper's text, read through a summarising fetch, states that quasiperfect numbers 'must be odd squares greater than 10^35' (citing Hagis and Cohen) and that 'With our method, we lift this bound to 10^45, which was established in about 440 core-hours (specifically, about 11 hours on a 40-core machine)'. It also says 'Existence of quasiperfect numbers is an open question.' The abstract says the method can 'significantly lift the existence bounds in open questions about quasiperfect and almost-perfect numbers'.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jan 2026 is the only version listed on the abs page as fetched.
events.delivers: A finite-range computation: no quasiperfect number below 10⁴⁵ (the paper says the bound is lifted to 10⁴⁵; it does not state the nonexistence theorem in that exact form). It adds no structural restriction beyond the known oddness and squareness, and it says nothing about n > 10⁴⁵.
events.remains: Existence of a quasiperfect number above 10⁴⁵; the existence question in general.
events.directly_checkable: The computation is in SageMath and its code availability was not confirmed by me; no hand check.
events.direction: A finite-range nonexistence result for quasiperfect numbers below 10⁴⁵; no object exhibited; does not settle existence above that range.

ai.disclosed_cost: About 440 core-hours (about 11 hours on a 40-core machine), per the paper's text as summarised.

events.what_happened: Akira Toyohara, Ye Tao and Siqiong Yao, 'Every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors', arXiv:2608.02066, math.NT, v1 submitted 3 Aug 2026 (CC BY 4.0). Theorem 1 claims: any quasiperfect number, if one exists, satisfies ω(n) ≥ 8, where ω counts distinct prime factors; this improves ω ≥ 7 from Hagis and Cohen (1982). The argument proves three algebraic lemmas that make a previously non-terminating search finite, then runs it: ω ≤ 6 is eliminated (their Theorem B4); for ω = 7 with 3 | n, a corridor search tree of 381 stems expands to 79,751,212 'deep leaves' with zero solutions; a single stem covers 3 ∤ n, ω = 7. The paper claims seven separately closed ledgers across CPU and GPU architectures. The lemma layer is said to be formalised in Lean (library qp_lean, 259 theorems, zero sorry, no Mathlib). Theorem 2 (not yet complete): if ω(n) = 8 then 3, 5, 17 are the three smallest prime factors, so 255² divides n; the computation for 3 | n and ω = 8 (516 stems) is 'roughly ninety percent closed by stem count' and is the start of a sequel toward ω ≥ 9. A conditional sector bound n > 10^26.38 under ω = 8 is given; the paper says it does not improve the unconditional n > 10⁴⁵ bound of [7]. The paper's acknowledgements say the mathematics and computation were produced in an AI-assisted workflow (see ai).
events.revisions: Only v1 listed on the abs page as fetched (3 Aug 2026). No later version found.
events.delivers: Claimed unconditional restriction: any quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors, established by a machine enumeration that is not yet replayable by anyone outside the authors. Theorem 2 restricts only the ω = 8 case (255 | n) and is stated as incomplete. Nothing here produces or excludes a quasiperfect number.
events.remains: Existence of any quasiperfect number. Also open per the paper: the ω = 8 structure (Theorem 2, about 90% closed), the sequel toward ω ≥ 9, and everything above 10⁴⁵.

checked_by.who: Pith Review (automated AI referee, recorded as 'deepseek-v4-flash')
checked_by.qualification: Not a human reader; an automated referee at the 'T0' level
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a 15 Aug 2026 review: calls the three lemmas useful and the write-up honest; says the main theorem 'rests on a 79-million-leaf enumeration that no one can yet replay'; lists three major objections (the three machine eliminations are not replayed in Lean; 'seven independent ledgers' overstates independence because several share one engine and all three architectures end at the same closed-form solve; the ω ≤ 6 verification is described less thoroughly); recommends refereeing and public artifacts. The page states 'No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.'

events.time_since_posted: about 2 months to 11 Oct 2026. The 'no engagement' flag refers to human engagement: I found no journal, no named expert, and no blog post. The only engagement found is the automated review above and a GitHub README (fderuiter/quasiperfect) that labels the claim conditional because the enumeration code is not public.

machine_checked.system: Lean library 'qp_lean' (19 modules, 259 theorems, no Mathlib, kernel decide only, no native_decide); covers the lemma layer, not the enumerations

events.directly_checkable: The three lemmas (discriminant criterion, quadratic-residue sieve, multilinear resolver) are described as elementary and could be checked by hand. The enumeration (79,751,212 leaves) cannot be checked by hand. The paper says its code, ledgers and Lean sources are 'available from the authors on request' and that a public repository is 'in preparation'; I found no URL.
events.doubts: (1) The main theorem rests on a 79,751,212-leaf enumeration. The paper gives no public code or ledgers (available on request, repository in preparation); the GitHub README says 'their enumeration code is not public'; the Pith review says no one can yet replay it. (2) Independence: the paper says 'seven separately closed ledgers', but its own §5.8 text says 'Ledgers 4–7 run the HC2 engine of ledger 3 under different scheduling' and 'all three architectures end at the same closed-form solve for the last free prime'. (3) Conflict on the 1982 3 ∤ n claim: the Hagis–Cohen abstract, as read, claims ω ≥ 9 and n > 10⁴⁰ when 3 ∤ n; this paper, as read, says that part was never published. Unreconciled. (4) The 2017 and 2019 Prasad–Sunitha results are not in this paper's bibliography as read. (5) Priority: Zemann's 2023 viXra claims the same ω ≥ 8 by computation; this paper calls its own enumeration the first complete proof and says Zemann's has a coverage gap. (6) Theorem 2 and the n > 10²⁶·³⁸ bound are conditional on ω = 8 and their computation is incomplete by the paper's own account. (7) The paper credits AI systems with the computations, the lemmas and the Lean code (see ai); this is a reason to rely on the artifacts, not a verdict. (8) The arXiv page lists no affiliations, and I found no other publications by these authors. I found no evidence linking this paper or its second author, Ye Tao, to Terence Tao.
events.direction: Cuts against any hypothetical quasiperfect number: claims every such number has at least eight distinct prime factors, and under ω = 8 that 255² divides it (conditional on the incomplete computation). It asserts no nonexistence and exhibits no object. The problem asks existence, so this narrows candidates without answering the question.

systems.name: Fable 5 model series
systems.what_it_did: Per the acknowledgements, 'AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series, ...) carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations, ran the independent verification ledgers, and drafted the text.' The sentence does not assign each task to a particular series. The authors say 'Ledger 2 was driven by a different model' without naming it. The paper does not say whether these are shipped or pre-release models.
systems.basis_quote: AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series, orchestrated in a multi-agent branch–synthesize–drill workflow with mandatory machine verification) carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, wrote and checked the Lean formalizations, ran the independent verification ledgers, and drafted the text.

Load-bearing on the paper's own account: the lemmas are what make the search finite, and the computations are the main theorem.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository fderuiter/quasiperfect, 'A hybrid formal-verification and high-performance-computation approach to the quasiperfect number problem' (741 commits on main; creation and commit dates not shown). The README: Lean 4 formalisation that 'any QPN must be an odd perfect square' (Cattaneo's result, formalised, not new); a Rust search whose 10⁴³ target is 'not an established result', with 'No lower bound on N is claimed'; the ω(N) ≥ 15 bound for gcd(N,15)=1 attributed to Prasad–Sunitha and listed as a 'conditional' result; and arXiv:2608.02066 listed as conditional because 'their enumeration code is not public'. The README cites arXiv:2601.17832 and arXiv:2608.02066, so its current text postdates 3 Aug 2026.
events.revisions: Current README dated only by its citations (after 3 Aug 2026); commit history not read.

machine_checked.system: Lean 4 (toolchain v4.30.0), with a 'lake build' the README says type-checks the proofs; the README also mentions Mathlib for a Zsigmondy formalisation

disputes.summary: Zemann (viXra, 4 Aug 2023) claims by computation that no quasiperfect number has fewer than 8 prime divisors. Toyohara, Tao and Yao (arXiv, 3 Aug 2026) claim the first complete proof of ω ≥ 8, and say Zemann's enumeration skipped 35 feasible exponents. Both claims are of the same restriction; the status of the 2023 claim is contested by the 2026 audit, which I could not verify.

The 1982 Hagis–Cohen abstract (read via the Cambridge page) claims ω(n) ≥ 9 and n > 10⁴⁰ when 3 ∤ n. The 2026 preprint, as read, says the ω ≥ 9 part of Hagis–Cohen 1982 was never published, and attributes an ω ≥ 8 result under 3 ∤ n to Abbott et al. (1973). These are not reconciled in any source I read. The 1982 full text was not readable.

The 1973 Abbott et al. paper is attributed three different bounds in sources I read: ω ≥ 5 in general with n > 10²⁰ (Graeme Cohen's 1980 paper, via a search summary), ω ≥ 8 when 3 ∤ n (arXiv:2608.02066), and ω ≥ 10 when gcd(N,15)=1 (Prasad–Sunitha 2017). The original was not opened.

summary: I ran 39 web searches, opened the arXiv abstract pages and the HTML of arXiv:2608.02066 and arXiv:2601.17832, the Pith review page, the GitHub repository, the OEIS entry, the viXra abstract, the Notes on Number Theory and Discrete Mathematics pages, the Cambridge page for Hagis–Cohen 1982, the Wikipedia article and the Wikipedia list of AI mathematical discoveries. The in-window events are: (1) Alekseyev's single-author arXiv:2601.17832 (25 Jan 2026), a SageMath computation that lifts the known lower bound for a quasiperfect number from 10³⁵ to 10⁴⁵ in about 440 core-hours, with no external check found; (2) Toyohara, Tao and Yao's arXiv:2608.02066 (3 Aug 2026), which claims every quasiperfect number has at least eight distinct prime factors, plus a conditional result under ω = 8 (255² divides n), with the computation about 90% closed and an unpublished sequel toward ω ≥ 9; (3) a 2025 OEIS candidate-sequence search bound, subsumed by (1); (4) a 2026 GitHub Lean/Rust repository that adds no bound and calls the 2026 claim conditional on unpublished code; and (5) a 2025 preprints.org/ResearchGate note, 'A Note on Quasiperfect Numbers', which a search summary says claims nonexistence. I could not open (5), so its content is unverified. None of these decides existence: no quasiperfect number is known, and no source I opened claims one or proves none exists. Wikipedia, as fetched, still states the bounds seven and 10³⁵ and does not mention the 2026 preprint or Alekseyev's result. AI: the 2026 preprint's acknowledgements, as read through a summarising fetch, state that the mathematics and computation were produced in an AI-assisted workflow, that 'AI systems (Anthropic's Claude, principally the Fable 5 and Opus model series ...)' carried out the computations, discovered and proved the lemmas, and wrote and checked the Lean formalisations, and that the human authors directed the campaign and reviewed the results. Ledger 2 is said to be driven by an unnamed 'different model'. By the paper's own account the AI contribution is load-bearing. No AI involvement was found in the text of arXiv:2601.17832, in the Wikipedia AI-discoveries list (which does not mention quasiperfect numbers), or in the Pith review, which is itself an automated AI referee (deepseek-v4-flash). Searches for the phrase 'branch-synthesize-drill', for OpenAI, Google DeepMind and AlphaEvolve work on this problem, and for Anthropic announcements on it, found nothing. Two close calls. First, whether the ω ≥ 8 result moves the problem: it narrows what any example must look like, which is a bound the statement does not ask for, and it is not a decision of existence; the reading that it is a first advance on the ω bound since 1982 (by the paper's account, a complete machine-verified elimination) is set against the reading that its main step has not been replayed by anyone and that no quasiperfect number is touched. Second, whether Alekseyev's 10⁴⁵ result is a finite-range check (like Collatz verification) or an existence bound (like the abc exceptional-set bound): the paper calls it an existence bound lift, but as a finite search it decides nothing above 10⁴⁵. The 2026 quotations come from a summarising fetch tool, since the PDF was binary and a direct download was not permitted in this session; I cross-checked the key sentences across three fetches, but they have not been compared against the raw PDF text.
competing_reading: Against 'nothing decisive happened': the 2026 preprint is, on its own account, the first movement of the general ω bound since 1982, and it carries an explicit AI-authored core; the 10⁴⁵ computation moves the numerical bound by ten orders of magnitude. A pass that counts a restriction every example must satisfy as progress would record a partial advance in 2026 with AI load-bearing. For 'nothing decisive happened to existence': neither event decides existence; the main enumeration is not replayable; the 2026 result does not address the 1982 3 ∤ n claim; and the in-window event that a reader can check directly is the 10⁴⁵ finite search. The 2026 claim does not contradict the 1982 ω ≥ 9 claim for 3 ∤ n; it is weaker there, but it says that claim was never published, which is the unresolved point.
what_would_settle_it: For arXiv:2608.02066: public release of the enumeration code, ledgers and Lean repository, an independent replay of the 381-stem campaign (or a sample of it), and a journal or referee decision; completion of the ω = 8 computation for Theorem 2. For the Hagis–Cohen 3 ∤ n conflict: the full 1982 text. For arXiv:2601.17832: its code, and an independent run. For the preprints.org/ResearchGate note: the text itself. For existence: a quasiperfect number (none known) or a complete nonexistence argument.
